questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Explain one-to-one counting using an early counting tool.
questions.prompt: A pupil puts one pebble in a cup for each basket delivered. Later the pupil pairs every pebble with a mark on a page. Explain how this method could help compare deliveries with a written list.
questions.answer: One pebble stands for one delivered basket. If a written mark or a pebble is left unmatched, the two records represent different totals.
questions.explanation: Pairing objects compares quantities without needing the baskets in front of the pupil.

markingGuide.description: Explains the one-to-one representation.
Uses an unmatched pebble or mark to detect a difference.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Differentiate manual bead tracking from a geared adding mechanism.
questions.prompt: One classroom model tracks a number by moving beads along rods. Another turns numbered wheels and makes the next wheel move when the first passes nine. Explain how the models handle a change from nine to ten differently.
questions.answer: In the bead model, the user changes the beads representing ones and tens. In the geared model, turning past nine mechanically moves the tens wheel.
questions.explanation: Both models represent place value, but the geared mechanism can carry to the next place automatically.

markingGuide.description: Describes a manual change in the bead model.
Explains the automatic carry in the wheel model.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an electromechanical counter from its operation.
questions.prompt: Each time a school gate opens, a switch sends an electrical pulse. The pulse moves a metal arm that advances a numbered wheel. Explain why the counter is electromechanical.
questions.answer: The switch and pulse provide the electrical action, and the arm and wheel move mechanically to change the displayed count.
questions.explanation: An electromechanical device combines electrical action with physical movement in the working mechanism.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the electrical part of the operation.
Identifies movement of the arm or wheel as the mechanical action.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a fixed-purpose electronic counter from a programmable computer.
questions.prompt: A sealed electronic counter increases a display by one when a button is pressed. A laptop runs an attendance program today and a drawing program tomorrow. Explain one capability shown by the laptop that the sealed counter lacks.
questions.answer: The laptop can run different programs and therefore perform different tasks. The counter is built to carry out the same counting operation each time.
questions.explanation: Electronic operation alone does not show whether a device can run different programs.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the ability to run different programs.
Connects the difference to the described counter and laptop.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish data analysis and software engineering in a school project.
questions.prompt: One technician studies a year of library records to identify when books are most in demand. A colleague builds and tests the program that pupils use to reserve books. Match each task to data analysis or software engineering and explain the difference.
questions.answer: Studying demand in existing records is data analysis. Building and testing the reservations program is software engineering.
questions.explanation: The first task extracts patterns from records. The second develops a tool people use.

markingGuide.description: Classifies analysis of demand and explains its purpose.
Classifies program development and explains its purpose.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Apply confidentiality when configuring a school device.
questions.prompt: A colleague asks the school computer technician for a copy of the pupils’ address list to practise formatting at home. Explain how the technician can protect confidentiality and still provide practice material.
questions.answer: Decline to share the genuine address list and provide an example file with invented entries.
questions.explanation: The actual records contain private information. Fictional records can have the same structure without exposing families’ details.

markingGuide.description: Protects or withholds the genuine records.
Provides a workable practice alternative using fictional data.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the jobs of the CPU and RAM while a program runs.
questions.prompt: When a drawing program opens, the computer keeps the current drawing in RAM and uses the CPU as the pupil changes its colours. Explain what each component contributes.
questions.answer: RAM temporarily holds the program data in use. The CPU carries out the instructions that apply the changes.
questions.explanation: The processor executes operations and working memory holds data that needs to be available quickly.

markingGuide.description: Explains RAM as temporary working memory.
Explains the CPU as executing instructions.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.subtopic: Retaining saved work after power loss
questions.learningObjective: Explain the different behaviour of RAM and persistent storage after a loss of power.
questions.prompt: A pupil saves a story to the computer’s solid-state drive, then adds a paragraph without saving again. The computer loses power. Assume there is no recovery or autosave feature. Which version should the pupil expect to find after restarting and why?
questions.answer: The last saved version should still be on the solid-state drive. The new paragraph was only in working memory, which requires power to retain its contents.
questions.explanation: Persistent storage retains saved data without power. Unsaved changes in volatile RAM can be lost.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the last saved version.
Explains the difference between RAM and solid-state storage in the scenario.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.topic: Basic Computer Hardware Components II: Storage Units
questions.learningObjective: Relate a bit to a byte in a representation.
questions.prompt: A pupil draws eight switches in a line, each with an on or off state. If each switch represents one bit, explain why the line can represent one byte.
questions.answer: Each switch represents one binary digit. A byte contains eight bits, so the eight positions together represent one byte.
questions.explanation: The two possible states can stand for 0 and 1 in each position.

markingGuide.description: Explains how one switch represents one bit.
States that eight bits form one byte.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.topic: Basic Computer Hardware Components II: Storage Units
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish total capacity and available storage when checking a file move.
questions.prompt: A tablet has 32 GB of storage capacity and 2 GB free. A pupil needs to copy a 3 GB file to it. Can the copy fit as it stands, and which number controls that decision?
questions.answer: It cannot fit because the available space is 2 GB and the file needs 3 GB. The 32 GB figure is total capacity.
questions.explanation: Storage already occupied is part of capacity but is unavailable for a new copy.

markingGuide.description: Correctly decides that the copy cannot fit.
Uses free space and distinguishes it from total capacity.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.topic: Basic Computer Hardware Components II: Storage Units
questions.learningObjective: Convert decimal kilobytes to bytes before adding file sizes.
questions.prompt: A practice folder has a text file of 375 bytes and a second file of 2.4 kB. Use the decimal convention of 1 kB = 1,000 bytes. What is the combined size in bytes?
questions.answer: 2.4 kB is 2,400 bytes. Adding 375 gives 2,775 bytes.
questions.explanation: Convert both quantities to the same unit before adding.

markingGuide.description: Converts 2.4 kB to 2,400 bytes.
Adds to obtain 2,775 bytes.

questions.subject: Digital Technologies
questions.topic: Basic Computer Hardware Components II: Storage Units
questions.learningObjective: Use binary storage units to find remaining space.
questions.prompt: A classroom storage model has 5 MiB free. Three audio clips each need 1,250 KiB. Using 1 MiB = 1,024 KiB, determine how much space will remain in KiB after copying them.
questions.answer: The available space is 5,120 KiB. The clips need 3,750 KiB, leaving 1,370 KiB.
questions.explanation: Convert MiB to KiB, total the clips and subtract their total from the available space.

markingGuide.description: Converts 5 MiB to 5,120 KiB using the supplied convention.
Finds that the three clips need 3,750 KiB.
Finds 1,370 KiB remaining.
